title: Characterizing the Predictive Impact of Modalities with Supervised Latent-Variable Modeling
one_liner: PRIMO predicts with missing modalities and measures, for each case, how much the absent modality could still change the answer.
lead: A multimodal predictor often trains on pairs such as image plus text or audio plus video, then silently breaks when one side is absent. PRIMO is built for that setting. It learns from complete and partial training examples, treats the missing modality as an unknown variable tied to the observed modality and label, and then samples many plausible completions at test time. Those samples do two jobs at once: they let the model average over missing information for prediction, and they reveal whether the absent modality would have mattered for this specific case.

problem.h2: Multimodal systems usually assume every channel is present
paras: Suppose a hospital model uses notes, lab values, and sensor traces to predict risk. In real records, one of those channels is often absent. A standard multimodal model has two bad options in that case. It can discard incomplete examples during training, which wastes data, or it can fill the gap with one fixed guess, which hides uncertainty.

Both choices erase an important distinction: some missing channels barely affect the answer, while others could change it a lot. A model that inserts one average completion cannot tell those cases apart, because it never asks how much the answer would move across different plausible completions. PRIMO is built to keep that variation visible, because the spread across plausible completions is exactly the evidence needed to judge how much the missing channel matters.

callout.html: When a modality is missing, you need both a prediction and a way to measure whether the absent information would have changed that prediction.

panels.title: 1. One channel is absent
panels.caption: Training and test cases often arrive with only part of the multimodal record.

panels.title: 2. Fixed filling hides uncertainty
panels.caption: One average completion makes every missing case look more certain than it really is.

panels.title: 3. Learn plausible completions
panels.caption: PRIMO learns a conditional model for the absent channel given what is observed and the prediction task.

panels.title: 4. Re-run the predictor many times
panels.viz_args: completion 1 -> answer, completion 2 -> answer, completion 3 -> answer
panels.caption: Each sampled completion produces one plausible prediction.

panels.title: 5. Use the average and the spread
panels.caption: The mean gives the final prediction; the spread measures missing-modality impact.

steps.b: Train on complete and partial records
steps.text: Use all available examples instead of filtering to only fully observed multimodal pairs.

steps.b: Model the absent channel with a hidden variable
steps.text: Introduce a latent variable, which is a compact unknown code, that links the observed modality, the missing modality, and the target label.
At test time, draw many candidate versions of the missing modality from the learned conditional model.
Run the label predictor on every completed example and collect the resulting class probabilities or scores.
Average the predictions for the final answer, then compute how much those predictions vary across completions.

paras: The paper changes missing-modality handling from single imputation to conditional simulation. Instead of pretending there is one best replacement for the absent channel, PRIMO keeps a full conditional model of what that channel could have been in the context of the observed data and the prediction task.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: predictive impact of the missing modality
hidden.name: predictive impact
paras: Predictive impact asks a direct question: if you could reveal the missing modality, how much could the answer still move? PRIMO estimates that by drawing many plausible completions for the absent channel and checking how much the prediction changes from one completion to another.

If nearly all completions produce the same answer, the missing modality has low impact for this case. If the completions push the predictor toward different classes, the impact is high, because the absent channel carries decision-making information that the observed modality alone does not pin down. This is why PRIMO uses a variance-based summary across sampled predictions rather than only reporting the average.

heat.caption: Darker means predictions move more across sampled completions, so the absent modality matters more.

reads.html: The model asks: if I filled in the missing modality in several believable ways, would I keep making the same decision or would I change my mind?
PRIMO measures instance-level modality impact with the variance of predictions induced by multiple latent completions of the missing channel.

paras: The method works because missing data creates two separate jobs. First, you still need a label prediction. Second, you need to know whether the absent modality could have changed that prediction. A single filled-in value can support the first job a little, but it cannot support the second one, because there is no full spread of plausible alternatives to compare.

PRIMO builds that full spread explicitly. The observed modality restricts which completions are plausible, and the supervised objective further shapes those completions toward versions that matter for the target task. This matters because the goal is not to rebuild the missing channel in every visual or acoustic detail. The goal is to rebuild the parts of it that affect the label. By tying completion learning to prediction, PRIMO spends modeling capacity on task-relevant uncertainty.

At test time, repeated sampling turns hidden uncertainty into measurable output variation. If all reasonable completions lead to the same prediction, the answer is stable because the observed modality already determines the label. If different completions lead to different labels, the answer is unstable because the missing modality still contains unresolved evidence. The average prediction is useful because it integrates over uncertainty, and the spread is useful because it exposes how much unresolved evidence remains.

stages.s: Infer a hidden code, which is a compact unknown summary of the absent modality
Decode many plausible missing-modality completions from that code
Run the predictor on each completed multimodal example
Average predictions and measure their spread
Final label prediction plus instance-level modality impact

math.h2: Prediction and impact from sampled completions
math.words: PRIMO averages predictions over many sampled completions of the missing modality, then uses the variance across those predictions as the impact score.
math.equation: predictive_impact = variance of p(y | observed modality, sampled completion_k) across k samples
symbols: the modality that is present at test time
the k-th plausible reconstruction of the missing modality
how much the prediction changes across plausible completions

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose three sampled completions of the missing modality produce class probabilities for mortality of 0.18, 0.20, and 0.19.
The average is about 0.19 and the variance is tiny, so the absent modality has low impact for this patient.
Now suppose three completions produce 0.15, 0.54, and 0.81.
The average is about 0.50 but the variance is large, so the final decision is unstable because the missing modality could push the answer in very different directions.

math.note: The average gives the best prediction under uncertainty; the variance says whether that prediction is dependable without the missing channel.

bars.h2: What changes relative to common baselines

charts.title: Single-imputation baseline
rows: Maintains prediction quality when one modality is absent
charts.note: One fixed completion cannot show whether alternative plausible completions would change the answer, because the model sees only one filled-in record.

charts.title: PRIMO
rows: Maintains prediction quality when one modality is absent
charts.note: PRIMO preserves uncertainty about the absent channel, because it carries multiple plausible completions through the predictor instead of collapsing them into one guess.

items.b: The conditional completion model is weak.
items.html: If the learned completion model does not match the true relation between modalities, the sampled completions are unrealistic. Then both the average prediction and the impact score are unreliable, because they are computed from the wrong alternatives.
If you draw only a small number of completions, the estimated average and variance are noisy. The impact score may look small or large just because sampling happened to miss important alternatives.

If the training label does not reflect the decision you care about, the model will learn task-aware completions for the wrong target. PRIMO will still focus on label-relevant uncertainty, but it will be the wrong label.
PRIMO is most useful when the observed modality narrows the missing channel to a small set of believable possibilities and the label depends on differences among those possibilities.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy two-modality classifier where one modality is occasionally hidden. For example, use paired handwritten digit images and short audio clips. Train a baseline that fills the missing channel with one average guess and train PRIMO with sampled conditional completions. For each test example with one missing modality, record the average prediction and the prediction variance across completions.
demo.metric_eq: impact_error = absolute difference between estimated predictive impact and the true change in prediction after revealing the hidden modality
demo.closing: The demo should show two things at once: PRIMO keeps prediction quality near the full-modality model when one channel is missing, and its variance score is highest exactly on the cases where revealing the hidden modality changes the decision.
